resources.string: The samskaras
The life-cycle rites, as the grhyasutras describe them. Each entry names the passage it was written from. Where the sutras disagree, the entry says so rather than choosing quietly.
Thirteen rites of the sixteen. Karnavedha, Vidyarambha and Vedarambha are missing because none of them is described in the grhyasutras this reference is drawn from.
Find an auspicious day
The rites of the fourth night after the wedding.

Paraskara sets them on the fourth night, towards morning, with the fire established inside the house. What comes first is a series of expiation oblations, to Agni, Vayu, Surya, Chandra and Gandharva, each asking that what the sutra holds to dwell in the bride — and to bring harm to husband, children, cattle, house and fame — be taken out of her. On what follows, the sutra gives two answers: after each monthly period, or as he likes.
The third month of pregnancy. The stated object is a son.

Ashvalayana names three rites in one line — Garbhalambhana, Pumsavana, Anavalobhana — and then describes the third month, under Tishya: after fasting, the wife is given two beans and a barley grain in curds from a cow whose calf is her own colour. Asked three times what she drinks, she answers each time, the generation of a male child. Sankhayana also sets it in the third month.
The parting of the hair. Four sutras give four times.

Ashvalayana puts it in the fourth month of pregnancy, in the bright fortnight, with the moon in a nakshatra whose name is masculine. Sankhayana gives the seventh month and only at a first pregnancy, Paraskara the sixth or eighth and also only at a first, Khadira the fourth or sixth. This entry follows Ashvalayana. The hair is parted upwards three times, and two lute-players are told to sing of king Soma, naming the river they live beside.
The rite at birth, before anyone else touches the child.

Ashvalayana has the father feed the newborn butter and honey ground with gold, before other people touch him, and murmur the production of intelligence at both ears. Here the naming belongs to this rite rather than to a later one: two syllables or four, an even number for a boy and an uneven for a girl, and a second name for salutation that only the mother and father know until his initiation. Paraskara instead gives the naming a day of its own.
The naming, on the tenth day after birth.

Paraskara places it on the tenth day: the father, having fed the brahmanas, gives the child a name. The sutra is particular about its form — two syllables or four, beginning with a sonant, carrying a semivowel, and built with a krit suffix rather than a taddhita. For a girl it asks instead for an uneven number of syllables, ending in a long vowel, with a taddhita.
The first going out, in the fourth month.

Paraskara gives it in two sutras and no more: in the fourth month follows the going out, and the child is made to look at the sun while the verse that begins “That eye” is pronounced. It sits immediately after the naming, in the same kandika, and the sutra names neither an oblation nor a fee for it.
The first feeding with solid food, in the sixth month.

Three of the sutras open this rite with the same words — in the sixth month. Ashvalayana and Sankhayana then list what may be fed and what each is held to bring: goat for nourishment, partridge for holy lustre, and so on down a short list. Paraskara gives the offerings that accompany it and leaves the food itself unnamed.
The first tonsure. The sutras give three different years.

Ashvalayana sets it in the third year, then allows the custom of the family instead. Sankhayana offers the third year, or the fifth for a kshatriya. Paraskara puts it at one year, or before the third has passed. This entry follows Ashvalayana. The disagreement is old, and the texts make no attempt to settle it.
Initiation as a student, in the eighth year.

Ashvalayana sets it in the eighth year, then offers a second reckoning in the same breath — the eighth year counted from conception. It gives the eleventh year for a kshatriya and the twelfth for a vaishya, and an outer limit for each: the sixteenth, the twenty-second, the twenty-fourth. Beyond that the sutra holds the right to learn the Savitri to have lapsed.
The first shaving of the beard, in the sixteenth year.

Ashvalayana declares it by reference rather than describing it again: thereby the Godanakarman is declared, meaning the tonsure rite repeated, with the word beard put wherever the mantras say hair. In the sixteenth year. The barber is told to arrange the hair, the beard, the body hair and the nails, ending in the north. After bathing, the youth keeps silence for the rest of the day and breaks it before his teacher. An ox and a cow are the fee.
The bath that ends studentship, and the return home.

Ashvalayana opens with what has to be got for it: a jewel, two ear-rings, a pair of garments, a parasol, shoes, a staff, a wreath, something to rub with, ointment, eye salve, a turban — one set for the student and one for the teacher, and if only one can be had, it goes to the teacher. The beard is shaved first. Then the texts are altered so that they refer to himself, and what was said over the boy is said by the man.
The wedding. The seven steps are what complete it.

Paraskara has the bride led seven steps northward, with the count spoken over them — one for sap, two for juice, three for the prospering of wealth, four for comfort, five for cattle, six for the seasons — and at the seventh she is named friend. Ashvalayana gives the same seven steps. The rite runs across several kandikas; the steps are what the texts return to.
The last rite. The sutra opens with an illness.

Ashvalayana begins not with a death but with an illness: one who has set up the srauta fires and falls ill leaves the village, going east, north or north-east, because the fires are said to be fond of the village and, longing for it, might bring him back to health. Only then does the sutra turn. If he dies, ground is dug to the south-east or south-west, the length of a man with his arms raised, a fathom broad and a span deep.
